topic: Hilbert argues that all sciences that produce lasting results ultimately supply material for mathematics, citing Einstein's 1912 letter to Sommerfeld, and proposes grounding logic in physical-mechanical considerations as an invariant kind of 'happening'; he then begins a thesis on applying the laws of probability to logic and mathematical statements.

triage.modern_statement: The note is cut off mid-sentence. The only readable claim is a programmatic 'thesis' that the laws of probability can be applied to logic and to mathematical statements. Read loosely in modern terms, that means giving coherent degrees of belief (probabilities) to mathematical sentences whose truth is fixed but not yet known. Today this is studied under names like 'logical uncertainty' or probabilities on arithmetical and first-order sentences. But Hilbert's example ('z.B. Max-', maybe Maxwell, maximum or something else) and his term 'Ω-These' are not explained on the page, so there is no precise conjecture to pin down.
triage.answered_by: No specific answer can be assigned. Later work on the general idea includes: Kolmogorov's 1933 axioms for probability (part of Hilbert's 6th problem, but these cover events, not logical statements); Haim Gaifman, 'Reasoning with limited resources and assigning probabilities to arithmetical statements', Synthese 140 (2004); and Garrabrant, Benson-Tilsen, Critch, Soares and Taylor, 'Logical Induction' (MIRI, 2016).

evidence.claim: Gaifman (Synthese, vol. 140, May 2004, pp. 97–119) treats the problem of assigning probabilities to arithmetical statements.
Logical Induction (Garrabrant et al.) asks what it means for reasoners to assign 'reasonable probabilities' to statements of logic, and gives a criterion and an algorithm.
Newer machine-learning work also proposes ways to assign probabilities to first-order sentences.
Kolmogorov solved part of Hilbert's 6th problem in 1933 by axiomatizing probability theory. That covers probabilities of events, not of logical or mathematical statements.

triage.why: The sentence breaks off right at the example ('z.B. Max-'), and the meaning of 'Ω-These' cannot be recovered from the page, so the exact claim cannot be identified. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Its link to the 6th problem (probability and the foundations of physics) is only thematic. The broad idea, probabilities for mathematical statements, did become a real research area, from Gaifman 2004 to Logical Induction in 2016 and later ML work. That area is still active, but it would be speculation to say any of this work answers Hilbert's particular thesis.
